raw.readme_excerpt:
# GPU unlock 1.1.1 — RTX 4090, RTX 4070 Ti SUPER and RTX 4060 Ti 16GB

New to this project? Start with the [copy-paste Quick Start](QUICKSTART.md).

This Linux kernel module enables the SM speed-select override before the stock
NVIDIA driver starts. RTX 4090 (`10de:2684`, AD102) support has demonstrated
approximately **2× FP16 and BF16 tensor throughput with FP32 accumulation**:

| Mode | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| FP16 → FP32 accumulate | 165.6 TF/s | 331.6 TF/s |
| BF16 → FP32 accumulate | 165.5 TF/s | 330.6 TF/s |

The override survived PCIe Function Level Reset (FLR), stock NVIDIA `615.78.08`
initialization and CUDA benchmarks. INT8, `dp4a` and scalar FP32 stayed near their
baseline rates. The original transaction preceded the repository cleanup; see
the [technical report](rtx4090-register-report.md) and
[original evidence](docs/evidence/rtx4090/README.md).

An independent owner run of revision `8855e7b` also completed the RTX 4090
transaction and NVIDIA driver handoff on Linux `7.2.11-arch1-1`. Matched
stock/unlocked measurements with NVIDIA `615.78.08` and the same 450 W cap
found FP16/FP32 instruction throughput **160.4 → 320.4 TF/s** and BF16/FP32
**159.7 → 320.2 TF/s**. All exercised numerical checks passed. Real cuBLAS
GEMM median throughput varied by shape: FP16 gained 12–34%, BF16 gained
16–20% at two shapes and was essentially unchanged at 4096³. These are one
matched run pair with the desktop active, not whole-application speedups or
an extended stability test. See the [matched evidence and limits](docs/evidence/rtx4090-pr1-matched/README.md)
and [testing workflow](docs/testing.md).

A separate cold test of the Ada port on one RTX 4070 Ti SUPER
(`10de:2705`) with NVIDIA `580.178.04` measured FP16/FP32 tensor issue rate
at **95.0 → 189.9 TF/s** and BF16/FP32 at **95.0 → 189.7 TF/s** under the
same 240 W power cap. INT8 stayed at 379.5 TOP/s. The stock driver loaded,
the NVIDIA RM getter reported full FMLA32 rate, deterministic FP16/BF16 GEMM
outputs matched exactly, and owner mining recovered with fresh accepted shares.
A second matched instruction benchmark found **TF32/FP32 47.49 → 94.51 TF/s**
(1.99×), with its FP16/FP32 control also near 2×. Unsigned INT4/INT32 stayed
at approximately **754.8 TOP/s** in both states. These are register-resident
issue rates, not application GEMM or inference speedups.
A matched, verified E4M3 FP8/FP32 CUTLASS GEMM measured **59.326 TF/s stock →
59.495 TF/s unlocked** on this card, a 0.3% difference. This single GEMM did
not show a meaningful FP8 gain; other FP8 kernels remain untested.
This is one card; the unlock succeeded on two cold boots and two ordinary
warm reboots, the last from a persistent EFI default. Throughput was measured
on the first cold boot. See the [2705 canary report](docs/ada-2705-report.md)
and its [sanitized raw benchmark output](docs/evidence/ada2705/README.md).

The AD102 payload and its debug-booter analysis come from
**[TOTORONG/AD103_win_unlocker](https://huggingface.co/TOTORONG/AD103_win_unlocker)**.
This fork integrates that published payload into
**[Zagitta/gpu-unlock](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock)**'s Linux module,
firmware generation and boot packaging. The payload is essential to the result.

## Experimental Windows contribution — Latence.app

A separate [MSI RTX 4070 Ti AD104 Windows UEFI reference port](windows/ad104-msi/README.md)
records one successful manual boot with NVIDIA 616.56 and matched cuBLAS FP16/FP32
**+80.1%**, BF16/FP32 **+76.4%** measurements. It is tied to one captured MSI Z490
profile; it does **not** add AD104 admission to the Linux module. See the
[report and limitations](docs/ad104-windows-latence-app.md). No firmware/Windows/ROM
binaries or automatic boot installer are distributed. Contribution by **Latence.app**;
original upstream credits and licences are retained.

## Supported targets

The module selects the AD102 firmware and payload automatically for RTX 4090
`10de:2684`. The original GeForce/CMP GA10

raw.description: A personal home screen for Samsung The Frame. A starting point to fork and adapt.
raw.readme_excerpt:
# CleanFrame

A quieter home screen for Samsung The Frame. Your apps, a photograph and the time, with an interface made for the TV remote.

![CleanFrame browser preview using the bundled Manrope font](docs/images/cleanframe-dock.jpg)

I built CleanFrame for one TV: my own Samsung The Frame, running Tizen. I'm sharing the code and setup notes as a starting point for other people to build on.

**Use it at your own risk.** Most of the work has gone into making it work well on my TV. Very little has gone into making it portable. The setup scripts reflect my computer, TV and firmware, so expect to adapt them and test the result on your own hardware.

I highly recommend forking it and building on top of it, ideally with a coding agent that can help you understand and adapt the setup. Start with the browser preview, make the interface your own, then work through TV installation when you're ready. Native Home/startup changes need particular care; the setup guide covers the risks and recovery steps.

## Try the interface

You need Node.js 22+ and Python 3.10+ to run the browser preview.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/nthnclrk/CleanFrame.git
cd CleanFrame
npm ci
npm run dev:public
```

Open [localhost:4795/home/](http://localhost:4795/home/). Use the arrow keys, Enter and Escape, or click the controls. App launches and Samsung screens require a TV; the preview reports that limitation when you select them.

The public preview uses the included Manrope, Geist and Newsreader fonts.

## What you can change

- Choose a List or Dock layout, with icons, names or both.
- Use a photograph, light or dark background, with a simple 12-hour clock.
- Adjust typography, focus and glass materials through the same Settings interface.
- Choose and reorder Home apps; discover installed apps on the TV.
- Select from fifteen wallpapers and save your preferences locally.

The glass and blur are rendered ahead of time. The TV loads the finished images and uses transforms and opacity for focus feedback.

## Use a coding agent

Open this repo in a local coding agent and give it a bounded change:

```text
Read AGENTS.md, docs/development.md and docs/interaction-behaviour.md.
Help me adapt CleanFrame. Start with the public-font browser preview.
My first change is: <describe one change>.
Preserve remote navigation, saved preferences and the ES5 runtime.
Run the source checks and relevant browser checks. Show the result.
This task is browser-only: do not connect to a TV, sign or install a
package, or change Home/startup settings.
```

See [working with an agent](docs/for-agents.md) for the TV setup prompt and the distinction between UI work, app installation and native Home changes. An agent needs local computer access for TV work; a hosted chat cannot reach your TV merely by reading this repo.

## Put it on a TV

Use the staged [Samsung The Frame setup guide](docs/agent-tv-setup-guide.md) to understand the process used on my TV and adapt it to yours. It covers the remote's Developer Mode sequence, official Samsung tools, your own certificates and app identity, installation, visible checks and recovery.

The signing and TV scripts are specific to my setup. Your agent will need to adapt the paths, signing profile, identity checks and installed-app IDs, then verify each stage with you. Installing the app and assigning the remote Home button are separate steps.

| Area | Evidence and limits |
| --- | --- |
| Reference hardware | Samsung QA55LS03DAWXXY / LS03D, firmware 2130.0, Tizen 9.0, 32-bit ARM |
| App installation | Signed installation and launch commands succeeded through 0.6.1. Latest rendering and remote feel still need physical observation. |
| App launch and Home | Netflix/YouTube launch and physical Home from Netflix were confirmed on the reference setup. |
| Still open | Normal power-on after streaming/Art Mode, corrected Smart Hub escape and native Art Mode destinations need definite physical checks. |
| Other TVs | No compatibility claim. This is Ti
